title: Restroom System That Works for Everyone
author: Ms. Sam
summary: A secondary science teacher diagnoses the classic classroom pile-on of bathroom requests as a problem of social contagion rather than student laziness, and then walks through the procedure she built to solve it. The opening move is analytical: one audible request interrupts the thinking of everyone nearby, and the teacher's audible reply signals to the rest of the room that the same privilege is available. She recounts two failed approaches, a rationed hall-pass system that punished students with medical needs and rewarded the wrong incentives, and no system at all, which produced ten to fifteen requests per class and breaks of thirty to forty-five minutes. The fix she settled on came from a Carousel Teaching CPD course on maintaining silence: a finger-based hand signal for each common request, and a nod or head shake in reply so that no part of the exchange is spoken. She pairs the signals with an explicit script teaching students that a request is not an automatic yes and that a refusal is a not-right-now recorded on a clipboard, plus a sign-out step that logs who is out of the room. The piece is a compact worked example of how a procedure has to be taught, scripted and rehearsed rather than merely announced.
points: The diagnosis is that the teacher's own audible reply, not the student's request, is what converts one departure into a queue of them.
A rationed hall-pass scheme failed three ways at once: students indifferent to the reward, students who traded health for it, and students with medical needs.
Removing the system entirely produced ten to fifteen requests per class and absences of thirty to forty-five minutes that other students then imitated.
Her signals deliberately omit a one-finger option, and the reply is a nod or head shake so the room's silence is never broken.
The script teaches that a refusal is provisional, logged on a clipboard, and released at a moment in the lesson when leaving costs less.
quotes: In the situation above, we are seeing social contagion coming into play. Social contagion happens when people pick up behaviors, feelings, or attitudes from other people around them.
Once the teacher said, “Take the pass,” other students began to think that they could also get the same privilege. If their peer could be excused, why couldn’t they?
Why do students want a break from the assignment? Well, thinking requires cognitive effort, and sustained mental effort can sometimes feel uncomfortable.

But what about the students that did not care about the reward? What about the students that did care about the reward and were willing to compromise their health to get it? What about the students that had medical reasons to use the restroom consistently?
I intentionally did not create a one-finger option. I figured it was best not to give students an easy opportunity to flip people off.
Notice that my “yes” and “no” responses are NOT done verbally. They are communicated through body language instead. This was intentional.
By keeping my signals nonverbal, I maintain the silence of the classroom and keep students’ attention on the assignment instead of the restroom request.
The goal is to teach students to make these requests at times when they are less likely to interrupt their own thinking or the thinking of others.
